explain.say: Rim brakes stop a bike by squeezing the wheel rim. It starts at your hand: the brake lever is a lever that multiplies your grip and pulls a steel cable.

explain.say: Friction between pads and rim pushes against the wheel's turning and slows it. The bike's motion energy turns into heat in the rim and pads. Wet rims have less friction, so brakes work less well in the rain.

faq.q: Why is the brake lever a lever?
faq.a: The lever pivots near the handlebar, and your fingers pull far from the pivot, so the cable is pulled with several times your finger force.
asks: How does the brake lever work?

faq.q: What do the caliper arms do?
faq.a: The caliper arms pivot on a bolt. When the cable pulls their tops together, their lower ends swing the brake pads in against the rim.
Brake pads are blocks of rubbery material that press on the rim. They are made to grip strongly and to wear away slowly instead of the rim.
asks: Why do brake pads wear out?

faq.q: How does friction stop the wheel?
faq.a: Friction always acts against sliding. As the rim slides past the pressed pads, friction pushes back on it and slows the wheel, turning motion energy into heat.
asks: Where does the energy go when you brake?

faq.q: Why are brakes worse in the rain?
faq.a: Water on the rim acts like a lubricant and reduces friction between pads and rim, so the bike takes longer to stop until the rim is wiped dry.
asks: Why do wet brakes not work?

facts: Braking turns the bike's kinetic energy into heat by friction.
Many modern bikes use disc brakes, which squeeze a disc at the hub instead of the rim.
